clue.text: Walks twice as fast with more room between the lines

blocks.note: to go twice as fast is to double one's speed, read as the verb 'doubles'
walking with measured steps is pacing

explanation.surface: Someone striding along at double speed, oddly followed by a remark about typing layout.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as DOUBLES PACING: one who walks twice as fast doubles their pacing. The pieces are taken in reverse of their clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: Double spacing on a typed page leaves a blank line's worth of gap between each printed line of text.

clue.text: Litter produced in high season

blocks.note: meat that is high has gone off
one of the four seasons

explanation.surface: Animals giving birth to a litter at the peak of the breeding season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' here means smelly and spoiling, as with game or meat, not lofty.
explanation.definitionFit: A litter is the young born to an animal at one time, so its progeny or offspring.

clue.text: She removes bloodsuckers by putting polish on your head

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the opening letter is kept
in a down clue, one piece put on another sits above it, so it comes first

blocks.note: to buff is to polish to a shine
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A beautician applying polish to a client's scalp while somehow ridding them of leeches.
explanation.walkthrough: Buffy the Vampire Slayer is the TV heroine who kills vampires, the bloodsuckers of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Buffy Summers, the title character of the American TV series, slays vampires, which feed on human blood.

clue.text: Lead, perhaps, in which you show your best

definitions.text: in which you show your best

blocks.note: first meaning: lead is one example of a chemical substance in the periodic table

blocks.clueFragment: in which you show your best
blocks.note: second meaning: being 'in your' one of these means being where you perform best

explanation.surface: Taking the lead in something you are good at, as in a play or a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' wants to be read as leading, but it is the metal; the second half is the idiom 'in your element'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lead is a chemical element, and someone at ease in their natural surroundings is said to be in their element.

clue.text: Eliminates waste by storing diamonds in stacks

indicators.note: what stores something holds it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: stacks are piles
D is the card abbreviation for diamonds, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A jeweller's efficient system of keeping diamonds in stacks to cut wastage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diamonds' looks like jewels but is the card suit, and its plural doubles the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To piddle is to urinate, a colloquial way of saying a body passes liquid waste.

clue.text: Labour party linked up to work together

blocks.note: to chain things is to link them together
people who gang together join forces

explanation.surface: The Labour Party members linking arms to cooperate.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital L makes it look political; read lower-case, a labour party is a work crew of prisoners in fetters.
explanation.definitionFit: A chain gang is a group of prisoners chained together while doing manual work outside the jail.

clue.text: Battle force turns to north when it's dark

indicators.note: one letter turning to another means it is swapped out for the new one

blocks.note: a battle is a fight
F is the symbol for force in physics
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: An army unit wheeling northward under cover of darkness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battle force' looks like one army; it is a word for battle whose F (force) becomes N, making NIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is the period between dusk and dawn, the time of day without sunlight.

clue.text: Optimistic view taken in the middle of drink

definitions.text: taken in the middle of drink

blocks.note: first meaning: the idiom for a hopeful outlook

blocks.clueFragment: taken in the middle of drink
blocks.note: second meaning: a tumbler caught partway through being drunk

explanation.surface: A drinker turning philosophical halfway down a pint.
explanation.walkthrough: Optimists see the tumbler as half full rather than half empty; literally, that is its state midway through a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying a vessel is half full rather than half empty is the proverbial sign of seeing things hopefully.

clue.text: Eccentric inventor swore: "This is our last chance!"

indicators.note: eccentric means odd and off-centre, so the letters are put into an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wild-eyed inventor cursing as the last window for his invention closes.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase urges seizing the present moment because the opportunity will not come again.

clue.text: Abandoned area of expertise that's not conventional

blocks.note: something abandoned has been left
one's field is one's specialist subject

explanation.surface: An unconventional subject that scholars have given up on.
explanation.walkthrough: From baseball, ideas coming out of left field are surprising or odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Left-field describes ideas or tastes that are unorthodox, eccentric and outside the mainstream.

clue.text: Dread finishing ultra marathon going less fast

indicators.note: the finishing letter of each word is its end, so only last letters are kept

blocks.note: the final letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A runner fearing they'll slow down near the end of a gruelling race.
explanation.definitionFit: Angst is a feeling of deep anxiety or apprehension, a close synonym for dread.

clue.text: Sentimental agent acquires old piano

indicators.note: something that acquires another takes it in, so one piece is placed inside

blocks.note: a secret agent is a spy
O is the standard abbreviation for old
p is the musical marking for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A soft-hearted secret agent buys a vintage piano.
explanation.definitionFit: Soppy is a British informal word for mawkish or excessively emotional, so overly sentimental.

clue.text: Duke is still a duke when gaining weight, initially

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it
the answer becomes the other duke only when it gains a letter, so that letter is taken off the duke's name

blocks.note: the Duke of Wellington, victor at Waterloo
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A duke who gains weight is still a duke, a jibe at aristocratic waistlines.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: add W to the answer and you get WELLINGTON, so remove it from Wellington to get ELLINGTON.
explanation.definitionFit: Duke Ellington was the American jazz bandleader and composer, whose nickname Duke stood in for his first name.

clue.text: Bob, for example, gets write-down of loan

blocks.note: first meaning: a bob is one style of cropped hair
second meaning: in finance, a reduction in the value of a debt that lenders accept

explanation.surface: A man called Bob has part of his loan written off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a man's name but is the hairstyle.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is a style of trimmed hair, and bankers call a loss taken on a debt's value a haircut.

clue.text: They talk most when the static is sorted

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; the definition describes those it fits

indicators.note: sorting things rearranges them into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Radio users can chat freely once the interference on the line is fixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Chatty people are talkative, so the chattiest are those who talk more than anyone else.

clue.text: A very desirable feature for coastal digs

definitions.text: A very desirable feature for coastal digs

blocks.note: surface reading: estate-agent talk for a selling point of a property
setter's reading: digs are lodgings, and a seaside room prizes what it looks out on

explanation.surface: An estate agent's blurb for a seaside flat.
explanation.walkthrough: Digs is British slang for rented rooms, not excavations on the coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Seaside rooms that look out over the water command higher prices, the most prized selling point of coastal lodgings.

clue.text: At home, constant strain sounds disturbing

indicators.note: sounds tells us to go by how the words are pronounced, not spelt

blocks.note: being at home is being in
constant means true, steadfast; a strainer is a sieve

explanation.surface: Constant tension in the household sounds unsettling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strain' looks like stress but is a noun for a kitchen sieve.
explanation.definitionFit: Something intrusive disturbs by forcing itself in where it is unwelcome, interrupting peace or privacy.

clue.text: Pull country girl back for being a slowcoach

indicators.note: going back means reading the letters from the end to the start

blocks.note: to pull is to drag
gal is a rustic or dialect word for a girl

explanation.surface: Someone tugging a farm girl backwards because she is too slow.
explanation.definitionFit: A laggard falls behind others, and a slowcoach is the British informal word for such a dawdler.

clue.text: Boring rubbish showing no emotion

blocks.note: a dead party or place is boring
to rubbish something is to pan it, criticise it harshly

explanation.surface: A dull person dismissing everything with a blank face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish' is a verb here, as in critics rubbishing a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan delivery keeps a blank face and flat voice, betraying no feeling at all.

clue.text: Lassie follows sailor!

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely
a tar is an old word for a sailor

explanation.surface: The loyal collie trotting after a sailor along the quay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follows' looks like the link between Lassie and sailor; it is the verb meaning tails.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassie the collie was a canine screen celebrity, famous across decades of films and television.

clue.text: Without moisture, river dropped and disappeared

indicators.note: a letter that is dropped is left out of the word

blocks.note: something without moisture has dried out
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: In a drought the river level fell and then vanished altogether.
explanation.definitionFit: A species or custom that died out ceased to exist entirely, vanishing from the world.

clue.text: It may be held when something breaks suddenly

definitions.text: It may be held when something breaks suddenly

blocks.note: surface reading: something gripped or kept steady
setter's reading: big news breaking, and the newspaper cry 'Hold the ...!' to make room for it

explanation.surface: Clutching on to something as it suddenly snaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks' suggests snapping, but it is news breaking; editors shout to hold the first sheet of the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Hold the front page is the newspaper cliche for delaying print so a late breaking story can lead.

clue.text: These body parts turn to fat

indicators.note: parts of the words means a piece taken from inside them
to turn round is to face the other way, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: the letters running across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A lament about one's body parts gradually turning to fat.
explanation.walkthrough: The run 'ESE BO' in the first two words, read backwards, gives OBESE.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means very fat, the clinical term for carrying excessive body weight.

clue.text: Timid type can think about nothing

indicators.note: one thing about another goes round it, enclosing it

blocks.note: to muse is to think or ponder
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A shy person whose mind goes blank.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouse is a quiet, shy or easily frightened person, named after the small nervous rodent.

clue.text: Butch eastern dictator takes in church

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside

blocks.note: Mao Zedong, Chinese communist leader
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A tough Asian strongman attending a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: Butch and macho both describe an aggressively masculine, tough manner or appearance.

clue.text: Fake news planted by gruesome extremists in Belgian city

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so the first and last letters are kept
planted by means set down next to, so the pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: fake news is a lie
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Extremists in a Belgian city spreading gory disinformation.
explanation.definitionFit: Liege is a major city in the French-speaking Wallonia region of eastern Belgium, on the Meuse.

clue.text: Condemn writer who works for money

blocks.note: a professional is paid for their work, unlike an amateur
a scribe is a writer or copyist

explanation.surface: Denouncing a hack who writes only for the pay cheque.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the reverse of their clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: To proscribe is to forbid or denounce something as harmful, officially condemning it.

clue.text: Standard fare Mike gave to wanted criminal

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so these letters are twisted out of order

blocks.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Mike handing a fugitive his usual dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat and two veg is the traditional British plain dinner, a joint of meat with two vegetables, typical everyday food.
